newsitem.title: HUNGARY: U.N. envoy calls E.Slavonia donor conference.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy calls E.Slavonia donor conference.

text.p: The United Nations administrator of Eastern Slavonia said on Tuesday he would ask donors next month to pledge some of an estimated $1 billion he says is needed to rebuild the last Serb-held enclave in Croatia.

"What we hope to do is to draw as many international organisations, national governments to Vukovar in December, brief them on what we think the problems are and then hopefully have them pledge," American diplomat Jacques Klein told a news conference in BUdapest.

Klein, who was in Hungary to discuss refugee problems and related issues with the government, said he would hold the donors' conference on December 6 in Vukovar, one of the most heavily damaged of all cities in the Yugoslavian conflict.
"The problems are quantum, as you well know," Klein said.

"We have a 60 percent unemployment rate, Vukovar is devastated. People say Sarajevo was shot up but Vukovar was leveled. There is no banking infrastructure, there is no currency flow, there is no economy.

"We all know that the future of the region and its reconstruction is absolutely essential if we're going to maintain any stability," said Klein, who administers Eastern Slavonia as head of the U.N. Transitional Authority (UNTAES).

The U.N. last Friday extended the one-year mandate of UNTAES, which was due to run out in January, until mid-1997. The U.N. body began work in February to disarm and stabilise the enclave and prepare it for a return to Croatian rule.
Klein said the enclave, which saw some of the fiercest fighting in the war sparked by Croatia's bid for independence from ex-Yugoslavia in 1991, was littered with up to a million landmines.
"We need the money to begin the process of de-mining," he said. "There is no technology other than probe and dig."
Klein said he did not expect to receive pledges for the full $1 billion, but was looking for at least enough to keep people fed and warm through the winter.
"I've got to feed people. I need humanitarian money to feed older people, an older population in Vukovar and elsewhere," he said.

Klein said there were significant signs of easing tensions in Eastern Slavonia. A market in the demilitarised zone between Croatia and the enclave had attracted 11,000 people one Saturday morning and 6,000 on another, without a single incident.
"There were people meeting, families, friends, some reunification, a little bit of business...The point is people are starting to meet each other. They're starting to have a dialogue," he said.
